analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its rules for banks and lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being introduced it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the 2010 law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the agency that writes and enforces rules for banks, credit card companies, debt collectors, payday lenders, and other consumer financial firms [S2][S3]. Wiping out the law would also revive the older, weaker legal framework those firms operated under before 2010 [S3]. In practice, the federal government would lose its main dedicated cop on the beat for consumer financial products. The bill went no further than being referred to committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, debt collectors, payday and title lenders, credit bureaus, and other consumer financial companies, which would be freed from the Bureau's rulemaking, supervision, and enforcement [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, credit bureaus

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 in full, which established the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau [S2][S3].
Restores the law as if the 2010 Act had never been enacted, meaning the consumer rules created by that statute would disappear and pre-2010 law would apply again [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers of financial products, who would lose the agency that polices mortgage servicing, credit cards, debt collection, credit reporting, and payday lending, and would again bear the cost of resolving disputes largely on their own through the courts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone who uses banks, credit cards, or loans

drawbacks.text: Repealing the statute outright would remove the Bureau's funding stream, rulemaking powers, and enforcement authority all at once, rather than reforming specific practices, leaving no federal agency with the same mandate over consumer financial products [S2][S3].

Because the bill revives pre-2010 law, consumers would give up protections built into the 2010 Act even where the underlying agency's mission might have been carried out differently under a narrower reform [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The concentrated benefit is clear: financial firms would escape a regulator with authority over nearly every consumer financial product. The cost would fall on households, who would lose a dedicated enforcement agency and the refunds and penalties it recovers from firms that break the law. The bill offered no replacement structure, so the trade is one-sided toward industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the Repeal CFPB Act on April 27, 2023, with four Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, its only action of the Congress [S5].
The bill's sole substantive section repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 and revives the prior law as if the Act had never been enacted [S3].
No committee vote, hearing action, floor vote, or House companion action appears in the record before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers keep the existing Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its rules; financial firms that lobbied for repeal did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; the CFPB survived the Congress

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the CFPB's founding statute and referred it to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Sens. Rand Paul, Kevin Cramer, John Barrasso, Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and all four cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led Banking Committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: Repeal would free them from the Bureau's rulemaking, supervision, and enforcement over mortgages, credit cards, and deposit accounts [S2][S3]. The Bureau's authority reaches practices like overdraft and junk fees that cost households billions, so its loss would fall on consumers.
These firms faced some of the Bureau's most aggressive scrutiny over short-term, high-cost loans; repeal would remove that oversight entirely [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: Both are directly regulated by the CFPB; repeal would end dedicated federal supervision of debt collection and credit reporting practices [S2][S3].
